# Calibration lab: three experiments on the bill-impact corpora

*Generated by `calibration_analysis.py` (seed 20260731); every number recomputed from the raw run records on each invocation. Input files pinned by sha256 below.*

**Summary for a demo audience.** (1) Letting the model author its own forecast distribution — five elicited quantiles instead of a point+interval pushed through the fixed interval_anchor transform — leaves mean normalized CRPS statistically unchanged against the production arm (-0.009 [-0.037, +0.013], 26 matched units), beats the transform when both arms get quantiles (-0.034 [-0.068, -0.003]), and relocates the miscalibration: the transform's tails over-cover (75/78 at 90% nominal, vs the model CDF's near-nominal 60/69) while the model's own 50% interval runs tight (29/69). (2) Across 728 cells the model's sampled answers spread far less than its stated intervals admit (median revealed/stated ratio 0.26; 8% of cells return the identical point on every rep) — and the bill text produces a double dissociation: fable-B's sampling spread widens (p=0.00344) with stated width flat (p=0.45), while opus-A narrows its stated width (p=0.00195) with sampling spread flat (p=0.85) — the bill can change beliefs without reported confidence, and reported confidence without beliefs. (3) A leave-one-unit-out interval rescaling fitted on resolved first prints by minimum Winkler score repairs the under-covering model (fable: 80% coverage 93/140 -> 109/140) at no proper-score cost (dWinkler -0.02 [-0.19, +0.14]), and does nothing reliable for the already-calibrated one (opus: dnCRPS -0.004 [-0.009, +0.002], n=28 units).

Truth = first print. sd_u = population SD of the unit's supplied history levels; nCRPS = per-unit mean CRPS / sd_u, averaged over units. Winkler score at alpha=0.2, normalized by the same sd_u. All CRPS/PIT via the house 201-point scorer (`scoring.py`, pinned against the TypeScript original; wiring re-verified against an independent numerical integration on real records — see self-tests). Sibling sweeps were still appending to some runs files at read time; the sha256 pins exactly what was read.

## Experiment 1 — model-authored CDF vs transform-imposed CDF

The production pipeline elicits point + 80% interval and *manufactures* the CDF shape via `interval_anchor_v1` (knots at p10/p50/p90 only, 1.5-spread linear tails) — so every scored distribution's shape is the transform's, not the model's. Here claude-opus-5 (effort=max, corpus B, no bill text — the measured-best base config) states p5/p25/p50/p75/p95 directly; the scoring CDF passes through the model's own five knots (same 1.5-spread tail convention, 201 points) and is scored by the unmodified house scorer against first prints. New runs: `quantile_sweep.py`, 3 reps x 28 units.

Gate (reject, never repair): 84 attempts; 69 scored; 0 non-monotone rejected; 0 parse failures; 15 API errors (all a workspace usage cap, HTTP 400, resets 2026-08-01T00:00Z; the cap fell on the tail of the unit-ordered dispatch — vetcola units — so missingness follows dispatch order, not response content, and the matched-unit pairing below absorbs it; `quantile_sweep.py` retries these cells on its next run). The non-monotone gate is exercised by self-test, so a zero there is a measured zero, not an untested one. Comparison arms from `runs_instr.jsonl`, same model, same effort, same base prompt: 81 `plain` (point+80% CI) runs scored (3 unusable) and 76 `quantiles` (p10/p50/p90) runs scored (8 unusable).

Coverage is read off each run's own scoring CDF by inversion (central 50%/80%/90% intervals); for interval_anchor CDFs the 80% row equals stated-interval containment (self-test 4). `pit-dev` = mean |PIT-0.5| (0.25 expected under perfect calibration).

Paired matched-unit nCRPS differences (model CDF minus transform CDF; negative favours the model CDF):

| comparison | matched units | delta mean nCRPS [95% bootstrap CI] |
|---|---:|---|
| model CDF vs transform(point+CI) | 26 | -0.009 [-0.037, 0.013] |
| model CDF vs transform(p10/p50/p90) | 26 | -0.034 [-0.068, -0.003] |
| model CDF vs bakeoff default-effort (context only: effort differs) | 26 | -0.024 [-0.067, 0.023] |

**Verdict on the pre-stated criterion** (beat the transform on mean nCRPS AND on |coverage-nominal| at both 50% and 90%): **not met**. The model-authored CDF is statistically indistinguishable from the transform on mean nCRPS (point estimate -0.009 mildly favours it, CI includes 0); coverage deviations are |0.080| vs |0.064| at 50% and |0.030| vs |0.062| at 90% — 90% favours the model CDF, 50% favours the transform. The two arms misfire in different places: the transform's 1.5-spread tails over-cover at 90% nominal (0.962 observed) where the model's own p5/p95 sit near nominal (0.870), while the model's elicited p25-p75 core runs tight (0.420 at 50% nominal) where the transform's interpolated 50% band is closer (0.564). The cleanest same-information comparison — the model states quantiles either way — is model CDF vs transform(p10/p50/p90): -0.034 [-0.068, -0.003], CI excludes 0: pushing model quantiles through the fixed transform is strictly worse than honouring them.

## Experiment 2 — stated vs revealed uncertainty (no new API calls)

Each cell = one (corpus, model, elicitation, context, unit) with 5 reps at temperature 1.0. Revealed SD = sample SD of the point estimates across reps; stated SD = median stated 80% half-width / 1.2816 (the Gaussian-equivalent SD; z = Phi^-1(0.9)). The ratio revealed/stated is a consistency diagnostic no single human forecast can produce: it compares the uncertainty the model *admits* with the uncertainty it *exhibits* under resampling.

N = 728 cells (504 corpus A, 224 corpus B); cells need >=3 usable reps. Gates (all negative-tested): corpus A 0 unusable reps, 0 outside the [0.1x, 10x last-observed] plausibility band (analyze.py:136), 0 cells dropped <3 reps, 0 zero stated width; corpus B 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.

**(a) Stated >> revealed, everywhere.** Median ratio 0.26 (IQR 0.14-0.48, n=728 cells); only 8% of cells have revealed > stated, and 8% have revealed spread exactly zero (the model returned the same point five times at temperature 1.0). The models *say* far more uncertainty than they *sample*: the stated-interval machinery is not just reporting sampling noise back — it admits information the decoder's own variability does not carry.

**Does the ratio predict miscalibration?** Spearman rho(ratio, mean |PIT-0.5|): all cells rho=0.209 (p=1.3e-08, n=728); corpus A rho=0.215 (p=1.1e-06, n=504); corpus B rho=0.115 (p=0.087, n=224). Cells within a unit share a truth, so the clustering-robust check aggregates to unit level first: rho=0.267 (p=0.096, n=40 units). At cell level, higher revealed-relative-to-stated spread goes with more extreme PIT — cells that wobble more than they admit are also the cells whose stated distributions the truth lands in the tails of; the unit-aggregated check carries the same sign but does not reach significance at n=40, so the cell-level p-values should be read with the clustering in mind.

**(b) Does the bill change beliefs, or only reported confidence?** Paired per unit, bill (`operative_only`) vs no-bill (`none`), point_ci_json arms. Primary test: Wilcoxon signed-rank on raw paired differences of history-SD-normalized stated and revealed SD — raw, not log, so the cells with zero revealed spread stay in (they are concentrated exactly where the bill collapses sampling spread, and a log-ratio test would silently discard them). Median ratios are descriptive, over pairs where both sides are nonzero.

| corpus | model | n pairs | stated: median ratio (n) | p (raw diff) | revealed: median ratio (n) | p (raw diff) | zero-revealed cells none->bill |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| B | opus-5 | 28 | 1.051 (28) | 0.286 | 1.200 (28) | 0.178 | 0 -> 0 |
| B | fable-5 | 28 | 1.000 (28) | 0.447 | 1.516 (28) | 0.00344 | 0 -> 0 |
| A | sonnet-5 | 12 | 0.792 (12) | 0.00195 | 0.551 (8) | 0.000977 | 0 -> 4 |
| A | opus-5 | 12 | 0.959 (12) | 0.00195 | 0.927 (12) | 0.85 | 0 -> 0 |
| A | fable-5 | 12 | 0.840 (12) | 0.000488 | 1.000 (9) | 0.156 | 3 -> 0 |
| A | haiku-4-5-20251001 | 12 | 0.926 (12) | 0.301 | 0.592 (8) | 0.966 | 3 -> 2 |
| pooled primary (B-opus + A-sonnet) | — | 40 | — | 0.133 | — | 0.0996 | — |

Reading the decomposition: the two sides move independently, and each of the three possible patterns shows up in some model. **Beliefs without confidence** — fable-B's revealed spread widens under the bill (median ratio 1.52, p=0.00344) while its stated width does not move (p=0.45): the bill changes what the model *does*, not what it *says*. **Confidence without beliefs** — opus-A narrows its stated intervals (median ratio 0.959, p=0.00195) with revealed spread flat (p=0.85): the bill changes what the model *says*, not what it *does*. **Both, downward** — sonnet-A narrows stated (median ratio 0.79, p=0.00195) and collapses revealed (p=0.000977; 0 zero-revealed units without the bill -> 4 with it): the bill acts as an anchor that synchronizes the sampled answers. (fable-A moves the other way on zeros — 3 -> 0 — so the anchoring is not even monotone across models.) The pooled 28+12-unit test, which averages opposite-signed effects, is null on both sides (stated p=0.13, revealed p=0.1): the honest headline is heterogeneity by model, not a universal direction — and only this stated/revealed decomposition can tell the three patterns apart, because interval width alone cannot see the revealed side at all.

## Experiment 3 — LOO-fitted interval recalibration on resolved first prints

One scale factor w widens (w>1) or narrows (w<1) each stated interval about its point. For each held-out unit, w is fitted on the other 27 units by minimizing mean normalized Winkler score (alpha=0.2; proper, so it cannot be gamed by width alone — coverage-only fitting was rejected up front as reward-hackable), then applied to the held-out unit. No unit's correction ever saw its own truth. Fit cohort: corpus B no-bill point_ci_json runs (the corpus-A sonnet grid cannot fit opus per-model, so the honest per-model route is LOO within corpus B).

**opus no-bill (corpus B)** — 28 units, 140 runs (gate: {'kept': 140}). Fitted w across LOO folds: median 0.84, range 0.82-0.85 (stable: no fold moves it materially); boundary hits: 0.

**Verdict.** For opus the LOO correction narrows slightly (w~0.84) and buys nothing anyone should pay for: dnCRPS -0.004 [-0.009, 0.002], dWinkler -0.03 [-0.12, 0.08] — both CIs straddle zero — while 80% coverage drops from 115/140 to 103/140. For fable, whose raw intervals under-cover (93/140), the fitted widening (w~1.25) moves coverage to 109/140 and improves pit-dev (0.273 [0.248, 0.297] -> 0.238 [0.214, 0.262]) at flat Winkler — recalibration earns its keep exactly where miscalibration exists. The cross-corpus transfer is the cautionary tale: w=1.73 fitted on corpus A sonnet no-bill (12 units / 60 runs) over-widens opus on corpus B — coverage 133/140 = 0.950 [0.900, 0.976] (over-covered vs the 80% nominal), norm. Winkler 2.29 [1.87, 2.77] vs 1.61 [1.20, 2.20] uncorrected — a correction fitted on one model's miscalibration transferred to a differently-calibrated model makes it worse.

The remaining ~152 observations have no stored forecasts against them. A cross-unit interval-scale fit on 2 normalized heterogeneous-unit forecasts would be noise wearing a method's name; the leg is reported as unusable rather than forced.

- `PASS  house CRPS analytic (uniform, y=0.5): crps=0.0833333333 vs 1/12=0.0833333333`
